bonds.title: The guide on Bob's Peak
bonds.busy: Not my hour, e hoa. I'm up here through the day and into the evening, while there's a view to show.

ranks.title: The giant's heart
ranks.invite: You stopped to look before you took a photo. I like that. Have you a bit of the {slot}? I'll tell you who's lying in the lake.
talk: See the shape of it, bent like someone asleep on their side? That's Matau, a giant. He stole a chief's daughter, Manata, and her man Matakauri burned him where he slept.
The fire sank him deep and the snow-melt filled the hollow. But his heart never stopped. Watch the shore: the water lifts and drops, every twenty-seven minutes or so.
ranks.fact: Lake Wakatipu rises and falls in a slow standing wave, a seiche, about every 27 minutes; in the story told here it is the heartbeat of the giant Matau.

ask.q: If those are his knees below us, at Tāhuna, where's his head?

options.reply: Āe. Head at Glenorchy, knees here, feet at Kingston. Eighty kilometres of him.
Other way: his feet are at Kingston. Head at Glenorchy, knees here at Tāhuna. Eighty kilometres of him.

request.ask: Take the gondola down and stand at the edge of the bay a while. Count the minutes between the lake's breaths.

ranks.title: Whakatipu Waimāori
talk: Did you feel it? It's small. You have to be patient with him.
The lake's whole name is Whakatipu Waimāori. Our people came through here on the way to the pounamu, the greenstone, up at the head of the lake.
My cousin drives for the taxi company. I've told him you're with me, so he'll look after you.
ranks.fact: The Ngāi Tahu name of the lake is Whakatipu Waimāori; it lay on the old routes to the pounamu, greenstone, found near its head.

gives.name: Aroha's cousin
gives.text: 25% off every taxi and ride in Queenstown

request.text: Walk out to the trig station on the point of the Gardens
request.ask: Walk out to the end of the Gardens, to the trig station on the point. From there Tāhuna looks the way it did from a waka.

ranks.title: The first gondola
talk: You went right out to the point. Good.
Nobody rode up here till 1967. Before that a man cut a road, one in four and a half in places, and there was a little chalet at the top for the view.
The first cabins took four. These take ten, and they've only been running since 2023.
ranks.fact: The first gondola up Bob's Peak opened on 17 November 1967, six years after a road was cut to the viewpoint; the present ten-seat cabins date from 2023.

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Try your eye on the town. Aim at a building, press G, and tell me how close you got.

ranks.title: Kawarau
talk: Not bad, for someone used to looking down on the roofs.
The Remarkables have an older name: Kawarau. Same as the river under them, and that river's the only way out the lake has. Every drop leaves by Frankton, down there to the left.
ranks.fact: Kawarau is the Ngāi Tahu name for the Remarkables and for the river beneath them, the only outlet of Lake Wakatipu.

gives.name: Aroha's names
gives.text: Bearings: you know the peaks by both their names

request.ask: Have you eaten? Go and find a cheese roll or a pie in town. You can't know a place on an empty stomach.

ranks.title: Tāhuna
talk: Fed? Good. Now you can listen properly.
Rees put his sheep on the bay in 1860. Two years on they found gold up the Arrow, and there were thousands of men under canvas where the mall is now.
But Tāhuna was here first, and it's still the right name. Say it when you tell people where you've been.
ranks.fact: William Rees founded a sheep station at Queenstown Bay in 1860; gold was found in the Arrow River in 1862, and the camp that grew on the bay was named Queenstown in January 1863.

gives.name: Aroha's introduction
gives.text: 20% more for every job in Queenstown

bonds.title: The Earnslaw's deckhand
bonds.busy: She's tied up and I'm off home for my tea. I'm on the wharf mornings and through the day.

ranks.title: Coal
ranks.invite: You've been watching the smoke, eh. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll tell you what makes it.
talk: That's real coal smoke. She's the last coal-fired passenger steamer working in the southern hemisphere, and the stokers still feed her by the shovel.
She was the lake's truck. The stations out west had no road, so it all went on her deck: wool bales, mail, the shearing gang and their dogs.
ranks.fact: The TSS Earnslaw, named after Mount Earnslaw at the head of the lake, is the only coal-fired passenger steamship still in commercial service in the southern hemisphere.

ask.q: What d'you reckon she's named for?

options.reply: Mount Earnslaw, the big one at the head of the lake. On a clear run you can see it from the bow.
Ha, no. Mount Earnslaw, the big one at the head of the lake. On a clear run you can see it from the bow.

request.ask: Go on, take a run on her. Stand at the rail over the engine room and watch the stokers.

ranks.title: Nearly scrapped
talk: Loud down there, eh? You get used to it.
The railways ran her for fifty-odd years. Then the Glenorchy road opened in 1962, the freight went by truck, and by '68 they were ready to cut her up.
A tour company leased her the year after, and she's not stopped since. Which reminds me: there's a box of her old photographs for Lucy at Williams Cottage. Could you?
ranks.fact: After the Glenorchy road opened in 1962 the Earnslaw lost her freight, and in 1968 she was nearly scrapped; she was leased for tourist cruises in 1969.

gives.name: Callum's errand
gives.text: A paid delivery along the lakefront, in your diary under Work

request.text: Take the box of photographs to Williams Cottage
request.ask: The box is by the gangway. It's in your diary, under Work.

talk: Lucy rang. She's put the launch picture in the window.
That was 24 February 1912, down at Kingston. Same year as the Titanic, and I know which one I'd rather crew.
Her first trip with passengers was the eighteenth of October. That's her birthday, as far as the crew's concerned.
ranks.fact: The Earnslaw was launched at Kingston on 24 February 1912 and made her first passenger voyage on 18 October that year.

request.text: Photograph Steamer Wharf from the lakefront (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Take a picture of the wharf for me, from along the beach. Photo mode. Mum wants one for the fridge.

ranks.title: In the pictures
talk: Mum says it's on the fridge. High praise.
She had the Queen aboard in 1990. And she's been in the pictures: they dressed her up as an Amazon riverboat for an Indiana Jones film. She never even left the lake.
ranks.fact: The Earnslaw carried Queen Elizabeth II in 1990 and appeared as an Amazon riverboat in the 2008 film Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull.

gives.name: Deckhand's timetable
gives.text: Lines: you know when she sails without looking

request.text: Come down to Steamer Wharf in the evening, when the lamps are on
request.ask: Come down to the wharf one evening when the lamps are on the water. That's when the old place looks its age, in a good way.

ranks.title: The long lake
talk: Good, eh? Lamps on the water.
Eighty kilometres, this lake. Longest in the country. Till the sixties a steamer was the only way to get to the head of it.
If you ever want a go on the shovel, I'll have a word with the chief. Wear old clothes.
ranks.fact: Lake Wakatipu, 80 km long, is New Zealand's longest lake; until the road opened in 1962, Glenorchy at its head was reached by steamer.

gives.name: A word with the chief
gives.text: Lines, from someone who works the lake's only one

bonds.title: The shopkeeper at Williams Cottage
bonds.busy: We're shut, love. The cottage keeps shop hours: mornings and through the day.

ranks.title: The boatman's house
ranks.invite: You wiped your feet. Nobody does. Have you a bit of the {slot}? I'll show you the house properly.
talk: John Williams built this in 1864. He ran a boat on the lake, and he built his house the way you'd build one: tight, plain, nothing wasted.
They think it's the oldest cottage left in town, and hardly a board's been changed. You're standing on the floor he laid.
ranks.fact: Williams Cottage on Marine Parade, built by the boatman John Williams in 1864, is believed to be the oldest cottage still standing in Queenstown.

ask.q: What do you think he built it from?

options.reply: Timber, every wall of it. Only the chimney's schist. He knew wood, so he used wood.
Only the chimney. The rest is timber, fitted like a hull. He knew wood, so he used wood.

request.text: Photograph the three old buildings of the lakefront
request.ask: I want new postcards for the shop: Eichardt's, St Peter's and this place. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: Rees's woolshed
talk: Lovely. You got the chimney in.
Eichardt's, on the corner, started as a woolshed. Rees ran sheep here from 1860. Then the gold came, and a woolshed full of thirsty diggers is a pub. He called it the Queen's Arms.
ranks.fact: Eichardt's on Marine Parade began as William Rees's woolshed, which he turned into the Queen's Arms hotel when the gold rush arrived.

request.text: Walk up to St Peter's Church
request.ask: Have you been up to St Peter's? Two streets back from the water. The stone came off the lake shore.

ranks.title: The flood
talk: Margaret will have told you about her grandfather and his cart. She tells everyone.
November 1999. It rained for days and the lake had nowhere to put it. One river out, remember.
ranks.fact: In November 1999 Lake Wakatipu rose from 310.5 m to 312.77 m above sea level, the worst flood in Queenstown's recorded history.

ask.q: How far do you think it rose?

options.reply: Two and a quarter. It was in the streets and right up to this verandah. The lake's only across the road, after all.
I wish. Two and a quarter metres. It was in the streets and right up to this verandah.

gives.name: Lucy's good word
gives.text: 15% more for every job in Queenstown

request.text: Have something to eat or drink on the waterfront
request.ask: Go and have something hot on the waterfront, where the water stood. Then come and tell me it's hard to picture.

ranks.title: Two oaks
talk: Hard to picture, isn't it.
The Gardens across the bay started with two English oaks. The first mayor planted them in 1866, when the town became a borough, and the park opened round them the next year.
ranks.fact: Queenstown Gardens began with two English oaks planted in 1866 by the first mayor, James Robertson; the gardens opened in 1867.

request.text: Walk out to the point of the Gardens in the evening
request.ask: Walk out to the point of the Gardens one evening. The town's lights come on across the bay, and you'll see why he planted there.

ranks.title: The Camp
talk: You went at the right hour. Most go at noon and wonder what the fuss is.
The town got its name in January 1863. Before that it was just The Camp, or Canvastown, for all the tents.
A hundred and sixty years on and I'm still selling things to people passing through. Come back and I'll put the kettle on.
ranks.fact: Queenstown took its name in January 1863; before then the gold-rush settlement was known as The Camp or Canvastown.

gives.name: An eye for old things
gives.text: Eye, from someone who can date a house by its chimney

bonds.title: The regular on the hill
bonds.busy: Wrong hour, or wrong weather. I'm up here on dry evenings, from the last of the sun till the stars are out.

ranks.title: The last of the sun
ranks.invite: You're facing the right way, at least. Got a bit of the {slot}? Stand here and I'll tell you when to look.
talk: The Remarkables run north to south, a wall along the lake. So the sun drops behind us, over Ben Lomond, and that whole west face takes the last of it.
First gold, then pink, then a grey-blue like a pigeon. People leave at gold. Don't.
ranks.fact: The Remarkables run almost north to south along the east side of Lake Wakatipu, so their west face catches the last sunlight of the day.

ask.q: So when do you take the picture?

options.text: After the sun's gone, at the pink
options.reply: That's it. Ten minutes after it's off the town, the tops are still lit. That's the one.
At midday it's a wall of rock. Wait till the sun's off the town and the tops are still lit. That's the one.

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Show me one frame taken in the good light: the last of the sun, or just after.

ranks.title: Night film
talk: There. You stayed for the pink.
Now stay for the dark. We're at forty-five south, and the Southern Cross never sets here. It just wheels round the pole all night.
I shot film for years, the kind made for lamplight. Here, I've set your camera the same way.
ranks.fact: At Queenstown's latitude, 45 degrees south, the Southern Cross never sets; it circles the south celestial pole all night.

gives.name: Night film
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out on Hemi's night film

request.text: Find the trig station on Bob's Peak
request.ask: There's a trig station just along from here. Go and stand at it and learn your peaks: Cecil, Walter, the Remarkables.

ranks.title: Ben Lomond

needs.text: Shoot a bit more first. Come back when you can tell me where the sun leaves the lake.

talk: Right. The big one behind us: Ben Lomond, 1,748 metres. A shepherd called McAusland named it, homesick for the one in Scotland.
You can walk it from here. It's a full day up and back, and the top is all tussock and wind. Take a jacket, even in January.
ranks.fact: Ben Lomond, 1,748 m, rises behind Bob's Peak; it was named by the shepherd Duncan McAusland after Ben Lomond in Scotland.

request.text: Show a visitor the way from Bob's Peak
request.ask: There's always someone up here asking which way's what. Help one out. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: One boy, two mountains
talk: You pointed them right. Half the town couldn't.
Those two across the lake, Cecil Peak and Walter Peak: that's one boy's names. Cecil Walter Rees, the runholder's eldest. He got a mountain for each.
ranks.fact: Cecil Peak and Walter Peak, across the lake from Queenstown, were both named for Cecil Walter Rees, eldest son of the runholder William Rees.

gives.name: Hemi's light
gives.text: Light: you know which face the sun leaves last

request.text: Be on Bob's Peak after dark, for the stars
request.ask: Come back up when it's properly dark and let your eyes settle. Ten minutes, no phone.

ranks.title: The southern lights
talk: See? You don't get that in Auckland.
On a strong night the aurora shows from here, low in the south over the lake. A green smear, sometimes pink pillars. You'll think it's cloud till the camera says otherwise.
Thirty years I've been coming up, and never the same evening twice. Bring a thermos next time. Mine's empty.
ranks.fact: The aurora australis is sometimes seen from Queenstown, low on the southern horizon, when solar activity is strong.

gives.name: Thirty years of evenings
gives.text: Light, from someone who waits for it

jobs.title: A box for Williams Cottage
jobs.blurb: A box of old Earnslaw photographs from Steamer Wharf along the lakefront to Lucy at Williams Cottage.
jobs.text: A shoebox of photographs: the Earnslaw on her launch day at Kingston. Keep it level.
jobs.done: Lucy has the lid off before you've let go.

jobs.title: Which way from Bob's Peak?
jobs.blurb: Visitors at the lookout ask what they are looking at. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: A couple with a folded map
jobs.done: They thank you and get their camera out.

jobs.title: Three old buildings
jobs.blurb: Lucy wants new postcards of the old lakefront: Williams Cottage, Eichardt's and St Peter's Church. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: Lucy props the three of them by the till.

jobs.title: A fare to the steamer
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up on Brecon Street below the gondola and get your passengers to Steamer Wharf before she sails.
jobs.who: A couple with a picnic rug
jobs.text: "Steamer Wharf, quick as you can. We're booked on the Earnslaw and she doesn't wait."

jobs.title: Mussels for the Skyline
jobs.blurb: A chilly bin of Marlborough mussels from the bottom station up to the Skyline's kitchen. The gondola is the quick way; the track through the trees is the honest one.
jobs.text: Twenty kilos of green-lipped mussels on ice. This side up, and don't let it slide in the cabin.
jobs.done: Rawiri lifts the lid and counts.

shops.name: Wharf kiosk
shops.hello: Kia ora. Cones or fish, what'll it be?

menu.name: Hokey pokey ice cream
menu.text: Vanilla ice cream with crunchy lumps of honeycomb toffee through it. It has been sold here since the 1950s, and nowhere else took to it the same way.

menu.name: Blue cod and chips
menu.text: Blue cod is the fish of the south, caught off Southland and Stewart Island: white, sweet and firm in a thin batter, with a wedge of lemon.

menu.name: An Earnslaw pin
menu.text: An enamel pin of the steamer, red funnel and all, with 1912 under the waterline.

shops.name: Pie warmer
shops.hello: Morning! Pies are hot, cheese rolls just out.

menu.name: Cheese roll
menu.text: A slice of white bread rolled round a cheese and onion filling, toasted and buttered. People down here call it southern sushi; it belongs to Southland and Otago and hardly travels north.

menu.name: Mince and cheese pie
menu.text: Beef mince in gravy under a layer of melted cheese, in a pastry case you eat from the bag. The pie every New Zealand bakery is judged by.

shops.name: Coffee cart
shops.hello: Kia ora, what are you after?

menu.name: Flat white
menu.text: A double shot under a thin skin of steamed milk. New Zealanders will tell you it was invented in Wellington; Australians say Sydney.

menu.name: Lolly cake
menu.text: Crushed malt biscuits, butter and condensed milk, studded with soft coloured lollies and rolled in coconut. No baking, and no New Zealand childhood without it.

events.title: Queenstown Marathon
events.text: A Saturday in the middle of November each year (14 November in 2026): 42 km from Millbrook, near Arrowtown, to a finish on the Recreation Ground.
lines: The finish arch is up on the Recreation Ground and the grass is full of people in foil blankets, eating bananas and not sitting down in case they can't get up.
They started at Millbrook, near Arrowtown, forty-two kilometres ago, and came in past Lake Hayes and along the lake's edge. Everyone who crosses the line gets the same roar.

events.title: Matariki
events.text: The Māori new year, when the Matariki star cluster returns to the dawn sky in midwinter. The public holiday is a Friday in June or July: 10 July in 2026, 25 June in 2027.
lines: Before dawn, look low in the north-east, near where the sun will come up. A small tight cluster, like a smudge until your eyes settle: Matariki, the Pleiades.
Its return marks the Māori new year: a time to remember those who died in the year gone, and to share food. It has been a public holiday since 2022.

events.title: The Earnslaw's birthday
events.verb: Wish the old steamer many happy returns
events.text: On 18 October 1912 the TSS Earnslaw made her first passenger voyage on Lake Wakatipu. She has worked the lake ever since.
lines: She first carried passengers on this day in 1912, the year she was launched at Kingston. She still crosses the lake on the same two engines.
Stand near the funnel when the whistle goes. It is steam, not a recording, and you feel it in your teeth.

events.title: Anzac Day dawn service
events.verb: Stand with the town at the gates
events.text: Each 25 April the town gathers in the dark at the Memorial Gates on Marine Parade; in recent years the dawn service has begun at 6.30am.
lines: Half past six, cold and still dark. A good part of the town is standing on Marine Parade facing the Memorial Gates, and the lake behind them is black.
After the Last Post and the silence, the parade forms up and marches to the Memorial Centre, where the wreaths are laid.

events.title: New Year's Eve on the lakefront
events.verb: Join the crowd on the lakefront
events.text: The town's free New Year's Eve: bands on a stage in Earnslaw Park through the evening, and fireworks over the lake at midnight.
lines: A stage on the grass at Earnslaw Park, a band playing, and most of the town between it and the water. It is light until nearly ten at this time of year.
At midnight the fireworks go up over the bay, and the hills throw every bang back a second later.
